**The Baseus Blade H1 (20,000 mAh, 100 W) is a good pick if you want one bank for both a laptop and a phone.** The search results only covered this one model, so I can't say it beats every alternative.

**Why it works for flying**
- It's about 74 Wh, well under the 100 Wh per-battery limit the FAA sets for carry-on power banks ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries)).
- Its 100 W USB-C output can charge a MacBook Pro, and it has 2 USB-C and 2 USB-A ports.
- It's flat (134 × 134 × 18 mm, about 451 g), so it fits easily in a personal item.
- It costs $89.99 (list $99.99) at Baseus's US store, with a 24-month warranty and a 7-day return window ([Dealectric listing](https://dealectric.com/baseus-blade-h1-100w-20000mah)).

**Buy it:** [Baseus Blade H1 at Baseus's official US store](https://dealectric.com/go/baseus-blade-h1-100w-20000mah). This is an affiliate link, so Dealectric earns a commission at no cost to you. Check the price at checkout, since it may change.

**Rules for any power bank on a plane**
- **Carry-on only.** Power banks can't go in checked bags. If your bag is gate-checked, take the bank out first ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7)).
- **Stay under 100 Wh.** Larger banks (101–160 Wh) need airline approval, and anything over 160 Wh is banned. If the Wh isn't printed on the bank, multiply volts by amp-hours.
- **Protect the terminals.** Use the original packaging, a pouch, or tape over the terminals.
- **Airlines can be stricter.** Southwest, for example, limits you to one power bank as of April 20, 2026. It must stay out of the overhead bin, can't be charged from in-seat power, and must be visible while in use ([Southwest](https://support.southwest.com/helpcenter/article/Traveling-with-lithium-batteries-e-cigarettes-and-lighters)). Check your airline's policy before you fly.

If you only need to top up a phone, a smaller bank is lighter and cheaper. Any bank rated under 100 Wh with clear markings will meet the FAA rules.
